rv.q: A quietly transfixing performance from Ayo Edebiri provides reason enough to see the Broadway revival of “Proof,” David Auburn’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony-winning drama, first staged in 2000. Ms. Edebiri won an Emmy for the TV series “The Bear...
It’s a lovely Chicago play, brought thrillingly back to Broadway life.
A quietly transfixing performance from Ayo Edebiri provides reason enough to see the Broadway revival of "Proof."
The cast assembled here is easily one of the best on Broadway right now.
Proof remains a scintillating play.
Add to that Edebiri, who, while not giving the career-defining performance Parker did, is nonetheless worth seeing.
Edebiri, on the other hand, plays Catherine as a sane but furious woman under a terrific tension, a level of silent agitation that we see even when she turns away.
Despite that strong support, though, it ultimately falls on Edebiri to hold the play’s center of gravity.
It gets where it needs to go; what it lacks, at least for now, is elegance.
As it is, the show comes off lumpy and soft, with the inelegancies of the text left exposed and its sharper points insufficiently filed.
Proof, 25 years later, pulls us in and grips us in a manner that might surprise even the author.
And so will everyone else who comes to see this stunning revival.
An altogether first-class production that speaks to the brain and the heart in equal measure, a winner in every way.
Broadway just got smarter and deeper thanks to the return of David Auburn’s Proof, a complex, curvy, and thoroughly compelling play motored by a math-related mystery.

On stage, in her Broadway debut, Edebiri leaves it to the other actors to carry the drama. That’s not a great choice, but it makes for an effective first act, because the other actors are so good. In the second act, Catherine becomes fully alive.
Her mix of physical comedy, well-timed quips, and heartbreaking reveals must be seen to be believed.
Proof remains the same appealing play that it was a quarter century ago, when it ran for more than two years and won three Tony Awards and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
More a competent production than a revelatory one.
A precise but passionless Proof.
But Kail’s spiritless revival fails to tap into the play’s specific collision of expansive ideas and fervid emotion.

Edebiri, who is onstage for most of the show, does wondrous work, shifting from depressed and lethargic to excited and game, as needed. Her Catherine is a fascinating enigma. Is she nuts? Brilliant? A bit of both? What is clear is the toll caregiving...
Auburn’s drama remains a sturdily constructed mystery that deepens as it progresses.
Broadway’s first revival of Proof brings the star wattage, but can’t find the current running through David Auburn’s play.

cn.t: Auburn's Pulitzer-winning drama holds up well in Kail's revival, with critics largely praising the enduring text and supporting cast, though opinion divides sharply on lead Ayo Edebiri's performance—some find her astonishing, others unconvincing.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.

vr.q: I thought this was a really great production and found it in remarkable shape for a third preview.
I think this is a great revival of the play... if you want a reason to see proof other than just that it's a great play, go to see Cara Young. She's so good in this.
